name: Center for Open Science (COS) / OSF
subcategory: nonprofit research-transparency organisation; OSF (Open Science Framework) platform, OSF Registries and OSF Preprints
origin_detail: Founded in January 2013 in Charlottesville, Virginia, by Brian Nosek and Jeffrey Spies; UVA Today covered the launch. The Laura and John Arnold Foundation was lead funder, giving $2.53M in 2013. The OSF platform was created in 2012. COS began with the Reproducibility Project: Psychology, then a cancer-biology replication project run with Science Exchange. Its IRS 501(c)(3) ruling came in 2014.
flagship_projects: OSF Preprints (2017) and community preprint servers PsyArXiv, SocArXiv and engrXiv (2016)
openness_notes: A nonprofit with a free-to-use platform and Apache-2.0 code (CenterForOpenScience/osf.io, 732 stars, 365 forks). It scores 4 as fully open science infrastructure under nonprofit governance. The 2026 narrowing cuts scope, not licence openness: no new projects from 16 Nov 2026, all projects read-only from 19 Feb 2027, and private projects to be removed later with 12 months' notice. Public content stays readable, and links and DOIs resolve indefinitely.
risk_events: Funder concentration: the Laura and John Arnold Foundation (Arnold Ventures from 2019) was the largest listed sponsor in every year 2013-2019, at $1.87M-$6.21M a year (peak $6.21M in 2017)
An NSF mid-scale infrastructure proposal, submitted several times, was not funded. COS says it would have covered the OSF resource gap for five years.

11 Aug 2026: COS announced it would narrow OSF. Keeping the full platform would need $4-5M a year, about half of COS's operating budget, and earned revenue (mostly several dozen institutional members) covers only 10-20%.
16 Nov 2026: no new OSF projects or components. 19 Feb 2027: all public and private projects become read-only. Private projects will be removed at a later date, with 12 months' notice.
Costs of free openness: 63% of projects (>650,000) were never made public, almost 200,000 users used OSF only for private storage, and spam prevention took more resources than expected
$450,000 committed to a continuity fund for public OSF content, with an expanded Internet Archive partnership planned
robustness: COS is financially stable as an organisation: 2024 revenue was $10.2M, expenses $8.8M and net assets $13.4M, up from $4.6M in 2023. It has SOC 2 accreditation (2023) and a Platinum transparency rating. The platform itself proved fragile: about 95% of 2024 revenue was contributions and grants, and when large infrastructure grants did not come, COS cut OSF back to registrations, preprints and linking. The Apache-2.0 code can be self-hosted or forked, and public content is protected by a continuity fund and Internet Archive copies, but the hosted service's scope depends on grant income.
physical_science_relevance: OSF is used most in psychology and the social sciences (its origin) but is multidisciplinary. Among its community preprint servers is engrXiv for engineering (2016). For physical-science labs its main lesson is about infrastructure risk: a free, grant-funded service holding 29 million shared files is ending new file storage, and COS points users to Zenodo (CERN). In our assessment, OSF Registries (preregistration), which continues, suits self-driving-lab campaigns that want to fix their objectives and analysis plans before running.
openness_effect_assessment: Being free, open-source and nonprofit, OSF grew in 14 years to more than 1 million users, almost 300,000 registrations, about 400,000 public projects and 29 million shared files, and COS's replication projects reshaped norms in psychology. But openness at zero price created costs without revenue. Private storage and spam absorbed resources, earned revenue stayed at 10-20%, and after the NSF bid failed COS cut OSF back. Open licensing protected the code (Apache-2.0) but not the hosted service.
key_takeaway: COS shows the funding ceiling of philanthropy-built open infrastructure. About $69M of contributions and grants (2013-2024, Form 990s), with the Arnold Foundation the largest listed sponsor every year to 2019, built the best-known open-science platform. Yet in 2026 OSF stopped accepting new projects because COS could not raise $4-5M a year to run it. Its response is instructive: keep the unique, low-cost functions (preregistration, preprints, linking), hand storage to CERN-backed Zenodo and others, and fund the continuity of public records. A lab relying on any single free open-science service should keep its own copies, with DOIs on durable repositories.

funding_total_usd is the sum of 'contributions/grants' on COS's Form 990s for 2013-2024 as summarised by ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer (EIN 46-1496217). It is a cumulative grant total, not equity funding.
The 2024 jump in net assets (from $4.64M to $13.35M) suggests a large multi-year grant recognised in 2024; the funder was not identified on fetched pages.
Wikipedia dates the OSF announcement to September 2026 (citing Nature, d41586-026-02598-y, which was behind a login redirect). COS's own posts date it to 11 Aug 2026; the COS dates are used.
Employee count was not found on fetched pages.
COS's 2026 posts give two figures for earned revenue: 10-20% of OSF's needs (11 Aug) and about 10% (14 Aug).
